questions.title: Why does DeepSeekMath start from a code model instead of a general language model?
questions.question_body: The paper says DeepSeekMath-Base 7B is initialized from DeepSeek-Coder-Base-v1.5 7B, and it also claims that code training helps mathematical reasoning. I am confused about what exactly is being transferred here. Is the idea that code pretraining teaches the model symbolic structure, long-range dependencies, or something else? Also, if code helps, why is an additional math corpus still so important? I am trying to understand whether the benefit comes mostly from code syntax, from program execution-style reasoning, or simply from starting with a stronger base model.

questions.title: How does the iterative fastText data collection pipeline find new math pages instead of just rediscovering OpenWebMath-like pages?
questions.question_body: In the data collection section, the first fastText classifier is trained using OpenWebMath as positive examples and random Common Crawl pages as negative examples. My confusion is that this seems likely to recover pages that look similar to OpenWebMath, rather than broad mathematical content. The paper then groups pages by domain, marks domains with over $10\%$ retrieved pages as math-related, manually annotates math-specific URL patterns, and adds uncollected pages from those URLs back into the seed set. Can someone explain why this procedure should meaningfully increase diversity rather than just amplify the initial bias of the seed corpus?

questions.title: What exactly is removed during benchmark decontamination with the $10$-gram matching rule?
questions.question_body: The paper says that to avoid contamination, any text segment containing a $10$-gram that exactly matches benchmark text is removed from the math training corpus, and shorter benchmark texts with at least $3$ grams are handled by exact matching. I am unsure what the unit of removal is here. Are they deleting only the matched segment, the whole web page, or the whole document chunk used for training? Also, since many math problems share standard phrases, how does this rule avoid both false positives and false negatives?

questions.title: Why did the authors choose the top $40$B tokens in the first iteration if the final corpus is $120$B tokens?
questions.question_body: The paper says they ranked recalled pages by fastText score and tested keeping the top $40$B, $80$B, $120$B, and $160$B tokens, but in the first iteration they kept only the top $40$B tokens. Later, after four iterations, they ended up with a $120$B-token corpus. I do not understand the logic here. If larger retained sets were already considered, why start with only $40$B in the first round? Was this meant to maximize precision early, or is there another reason related to bootstrapping the classifier?

questions.title: Why would math pretraining improve MMLU and BBH, but mixing code and math can hurt some non-tool reasoning?
questions.question_body: The paper reports that math pretraining improves not only math benchmarks but also MMLU and BBH, which sounds like broader reasoning transfer. But later, in the discussion, they say that one-stage training on mixed code and math tokens can compromise mathematical reasoning without tool use, possibly because a $1.3$B model cannot absorb both well at once. I am confused about the connection. If math and code both help reasoning, why does combining them sometimes make performance worse? Is this mostly a capacity issue, a data distribution issue, or an optimization issue?

questions.title: Why do arXiv papers seem ineffective for mathematical reasoning in this paper?
questions.question_body: A result that surprised me is the claim that arXiv-only training gives no notable improvement, and can even hurt, on GSM8K, MATH, MMLU-STEM, and miniF2F. I would have expected math papers to be useful for mathematical ability. Is the issue that arXiv mostly contains exposition and formalism rather than step-by-step problem solving? Or is it that the style of benchmark questions is very different from research papers? I am trying to understand whether this result is about the domain mismatch, the cleaning pipeline, the model scale, or something deeper about how language models learn reasoning.

questions.title: In GRPO, why is the same normalized reward assigned to every token under outcome supervision?
questions.question_body: For outcome-supervised GRPO, the paper sets the token-level advantage to the same value for all tokens in an output: $\hat{A}_{i,t} = \widetilde{r}_i = \frac{r_i - \mathrm{mean}(\mathbf{r})}{\mathrm{std}(\mathbf{r})}$. I am struggling with the credit assignment intuition here. If only the final answer is scored, why is it reasonable to reinforce every token equally, including early setup text that may not have contributed much? Is this just a practical approximation because the reward exists only at the end, or is there a stronger theoretical reason?

questions.title: How is GRPO's group-relative baseline better than a learned value function when all sampled answers for a question are poor?
questions.question_body: The paper motivates GRPO by removing the critic and using the average reward within a sampled group as a baseline. I understand the memory advantage, but I am confused about the statistical tradeoff. Suppose a question is hard and all $G$ sampled outputs are wrong or low-quality. Then the group mean is also poor, and one bad output could still receive a positive normalized advantage just because it is less bad than the others. Does GRPO then only learn relative ranking within the group rather than absolute quality? If so, why does this not cause drift or reinforce mediocre solutions?

questions.title: What is the practical difference between adding KL regularization to the reward and adding a KL term directly to the GRPO objective?
questions.question_body: In the PPO discussion, the paper uses a per-token reward of the form $r_t = r_\varphi(q, o_{\le t}) - \beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(o_t \mid q, o_{<t})}{\pi_{ref}(o_t \mid q, o_{<t})}$. In GRPO, instead of folding the KL penalty into the reward, they subtract a KL divergence term directly in the objective, and they use a particular unbiased estimator. I do not see clearly why this change matters beyond implementation convenience. Does moving the KL term outside the reward alter the optimization dynamics, or is it mainly to keep the group-relative advantage $\hat{A}_{i,t}$ easy to compute and interpret?

questions.title: How should I interpret the process-supervision advantage $\hat{A}_{i,t} = \sum_{\mathrm{index}(j) \ge t} \widetilde{r}_i^{\mathrm{index}(j)}$ in GRPO?
questions.question_body: For process-supervised GRPO, the paper scores individual reasoning steps and defines each token's advantage as the sum of normalized rewards from all future step endpoints. This looks similar to a return in reinforcement learning, but I am not sure I understand the exact intuition. Why sum all future step rewards instead of using only the nearest step reward, or discounting them? Also, since the step rewards are normalized across the sampled outputs, does this mean the reward attached to one step depends on what other completions in the same group did?

questions.title: In what precise sense are DPO, RFT, PPO, and GRPO all part of one 'unified RL paradigm'?
questions.question_body:
The paper writes the gradient of several training methods in the common form

$\nabla_{\theta} \mathcal{J}_{\mathcal{A}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{(q,o) \sim \mathcal{D}} \left[ \frac{1}{|o|} \sum_{t=1}^{|o|} GC_{\mathcal{A}}(q, o, t, \pi_{rf}) \nabla_{\theta} \log \pi_{\theta}(o_t \mid q, o_{<t}) \right].$

I can see this as a formal rewriting, but I am not sure when it is actually insightful rather than just notational. For example, DPO is usually presented as supervised preference optimization, not RL in the usual online sense. So what is the substantive claim here? Is the paper saying these methods are equivalent, approximately equivalent, or just structurally comparable after choosing different data sources and gradient coefficients?

questions.title: Why does reinforcement learning improve $\mathrm{Maj}@K$ but not $\mathrm{Pass}@K$, and what does that imply about 'reasoning ability'?
questions.question_body: One of the most interesting claims in the discussion is that RL improves $\mathrm{Maj}@K$ but not $\mathrm{Pass}@K$, and the authors interpret this as making the output distribution more robust rather than improving fundamental capability. I am not fully convinced I understand this. If $\mathrm{Pass}@K$ stays the same, does that mean the model already knew how to solve those problems before RL, but RL only makes correct solutions more likely? If so, should RL here be viewed more as calibration or preference shaping than as learning new reasoning skills? I would appreciate an explanation of how to read these two metrics together.

questions.title: Why does online sampling help more than offline sampling in the later stages of training?
questions.question_body: In the unified-paradigm analysis, the paper says Online RFT eventually outperforms offline RFT because the actor diverges from the initial SFT model over time, so real-time samples become more informative. I follow this intuitively, but I am missing a sharper explanation. Is the main issue distribution shift, where the offline dataset stops representing the model being optimized? Or is it that online sampling naturally creates a curriculum by exposing the reward model and policy to progressively harder or more varied outputs? I want to understand exactly what advantage online data provides that offline augmented data cannot.

questions.title: How can GRPO be more memory-efficient than PPO if it samples $64$ outputs per question?
questions.question_body: The paper emphasizes that GRPO saves memory by removing the critic model, which makes sense. But in the RL setup they also sample $64$ outputs for each question, and that sounds expensive in its own right. I am confused about where the actual savings come from. Is the claim specifically about training-time parameter memory because there is no separate value network, while the large group size mainly affects inference-like rollout cost? In other words, what is the right apples-to-apples comparison between PPO and GRPO in terms of memory and compute?
